findings.topic: pharos-mcp v0.2.0/v0.3.0 plans: daemon mode, HTTPS/TLS, and the WebSocket editor bridge — transport implications for geex
findings.summary: pharos-mcp's roadmap splits three transport concerns across two milestones. v0.2.0 item #3 ("pharos as a service") adds a persistent daemon (`pharos daemon --port 8080` or a unix socket discoverable at `~/.local/share/pharos/daemon.sock`) plus HTTPS/TLS via `mist.with_tls`, bundled in one ADR because exposing pharos beyond localhost is what makes TLS load-bearing. The daemon exists to amortize slow LSP bootstrap (Java/Python/TS indexes that take minutes) across MCP host sessions; lifecycle decouples from stdin EOF and exits on idle-timeout instead, with the stdio command auto-discovering a running daemon or falling back to spawning an ephemeral per-session instance. The WebSocket "bridge" (v0.3.0+, ADR-028, status Proposed) is a bidirectional protocol where EDITOR PLUGINS push editor-side state (open buffers, cursor, selection, focus) to pharos so LSP queries reflect unsaved edits — it is built from scratch at `src/pharos/bridge/` (which does NOT exist yet; nor does the ADR file). The most geex-relevant conclusion: geex, as a first-party editor running on the same BEAM as pharos (Gleam→BEAM, geex is an Elixir OTP app), does NOT need the WebSocket bridge at all — it gets in-VM Erlang message passing / direct process calls to the shared LSP Pool for free, skipping serialization, the WebSocket handshake, TLS, and the entire plugin-conformance contract that out-of-VM editors (VSCode/Neovim/Zed) must implement.
findings.how_it_works:
DAEMON MODEL (roadmap §v0.2.0 item 3, lines 53-75). Working ADR title "pharos as a service." New CLI mode `pharos daemon --port 8080` (TCP) or a unix socket. Three lifecycle/discovery mechanics: (a) Lifecycle decoupling — today the process exits on stdin EOF (stdio MCP convention); the daemon instead does NOT exit on EOF and exits on an idle-timeout, so it survives across MCP host sessions. (b) Discovery via a well-known path `~/.local/share/pharos/daemon.sock`. The existing `pharos` stdio command auto-discovers the daemon if that socket is present and routes to it; otherwise it spawns a per-session ephemeral instance — graceful fallback, no hard dependency on a running daemon. (c) Multi-session HTTP routing is "mostly free" because the LSP pool key ALREADY includes workspace (pool keyed by `(language, workspace, server_id)` per ADR-017a, roadmap line 14), so cross-session sharing of warm LSP servers falls out of the existing design. WHY a daemon: closes "the biggest visible gap with prior-art persistent daemons for slow-bootstrap languages (Java / Python / TypeScript indexes that take minutes)" — the whole point is amortizing multi-minute LSP index warmup across sessions. Lift: medium (~300-500 LOC + an ADR).

HTTPS/TLS (same roadmap item, lines 67-70). TLS via `mist.with_tls(builder, cert, key)` — pharos's HTTP transport is already built on `mist` (confirmed in src/pharos/mcp/http.gleam: `mist.new(handler) |> mist.bind(bind) |> mist.port(port) |> mist.start()`), so adding TLS is layering one builder call onto the existing mist pipeline. New config in `pharos.toml [lsp.http]`: `tls_cert_file` / `tls_key_file`. CLI overrides `--tls-cert` / `--tls-key`. `pharos --doctor` gets a probe for cert/key file existence + permissions. CRITICAL framing: daemon and TLS share one ADR specifically because "exposing pharos beyond localhost is what makes TLS load-bearing" (line 57). Current state (roadmap line 23, confirmed in http.gleam header): HTTP transport is localhost-only and PLAIN — Origin-header validation guards DNS-rebinding but there is no transport encryption. TLS only becomes necessary once the daemon binds beyond loopback. For localhost-only use TLS is dead weight.

WEBSOCKET BRIDGE (roadmap §v0.3.0+, lines 125-182; ADR-028 "Universal editor bridge", status Proposed — and NOTE: I verified the ADR file `028-universal-editor-bridge.md` does NOT exist in .private/adr/, and `src/pharos/bridge/` does NOT exist either; roadmap line 173-176 explicitly says "ADR-028 references a stub at this path that does not exist yet — the implementation starts from zero"). SHAPE: a WebSocket server inside pharos at `src/pharos/bridge/` doing handshake, capability negotiation, `didOpen`/`didChange` ingestion, and forwarding to the LSP pool. Bidirectional: editor→pharos pushes live editor state; pharos→editor reverse channel for diff-preview, diagnostics, progress. PROBLEM IT SOLVES: LSP-over-disk can only see saved files; the bridge lets editor plugins push cursor location, unsaved buffer contents, focus, and selection so pharos's LSPs/tools can answer questions disk state can't reach — e.g. queries that must reflect un-saved edits, plus an `editor_focus()` MCP tool (Tier 2) letting the LLM ask "what is the user looking at?" in one call. FIVE TIERS (implementation-ordered): (1) Live document mirroring — didOpen/didChange/didSave/didClose; mandatory, bridge not worth shipping without it; (2) Focus-context tool `editor_focus()` returning active URI + cursor + selection + viewport + open-file list; (3) Diff-preview UX — pharos asks editor to render a WorkspaceEdit as a diff, commits on accept (human-in-loop refactors); (4) Diagnostics surfacing into the editor's native Problems panel; (5) Progress reporting into native progress UI. PLUGIN MODEL: plugins live in separate repos named `pharos-<editor>` (pharos-vscode ~200 LOC TS ships first, pharos-neovim ~150 LOC Lua, pharos-zed ~300 LOC Rust/WASM, emacs ~150 LOC Elisp, JetBrains ~500 LOC Kotlin, Sublime ~200 LOC Python). NO build-time coupling: pharos owns the protocol spec (`doc/bridge-protocol.md`, versioned) + a conformance tester (`bin/test-plugin-conformance.*`); plugins implement the JSON contract in their host language. Pharos-side surface: build the bridge WebSocket server, add `editor_focus` tool, wire reverse-channel `showDiff` into `apply_workspace_edit`, publish the spec, ship the conformance harness, build pharos-vscode as reference impl in its own repo.

GEEX RELATIONSHIP (the load-bearing analysis). geex is an Elixir OTP application (mix.exs: `mod: {Geex.Application, []}`, elixir ~> 1.18). pharos is Gleam — which compiles to BEAM and runs OTP (the roadmap repeatedly cites "BEAM/OTP-supervised LSP pool", gleam/otp actors and static_supervisor in http.gleam). Therefore geex and pharos can run on (or interop across) the SAME BEAM VM. The bridge's entire reason for existing is to get editor-side state INTO pharos across a process/host boundary that requires serialization + a socket + a handshake + a versioned wire spec + per-language plugins + conformance testing + (eventually) TLS. A first-party editor co-located on the BEAM sidesteps that whole stack: it can deliver `didOpen`/`didChange`/focus/selection as native Erlang messages (`send`/`GenServer.call`/`:gen_statem`) directly to pharos's LSP pool processes, and read results back as terms — no JSON encoding, no WebSocket frame, no handshake/capability negotiation, no TLS, no `pharos-geex` plugin repo. The pool is already a shared in-VM resource (one Pool shared between stdio and HTTP transports, keyed by workspace), so geex would attach to the same warm LSP servers the daemon model is built to share. Net: geex likely needs NONE of the bridge transport machinery; it wants the bridge's SEMANTIC contract (the set of editor-state messages and the editor_focus shape) but realized as an in-VM API, not a WebSocket.

key_concepts.name: daemon discovery + graceful fallback
key_concepts.what: Well-known socket at ~/.local/share/pharos/daemon.sock. The stdio `pharos` command auto-discovers and routes to a running daemon if present, else spawns an ephemeral per-session instance. No hard dependency on the daemon.

key_concepts.name: workspace-keyed pool = free multi-session sharing
key_concepts.what: LSP pool key already includes workspace (`(language, workspace, server_id)`, ADR-017a), so cross-session HTTP routing and warm-server sharing under the daemon are 'mostly free' — no new keying work.

key_concepts.name: mist.with_tls
key_concepts.what: v0.2.0 TLS path: layer `mist.with_tls(builder, cert, key)` onto the existing mist HTTP builder. Config `pharos.toml [lsp.http] tls_cert_file`/`tls_key_file`, CLI `--tls-cert`/`--tls-key`, doctor probe for file existence/perms.

key_concepts.name: TLS is load-bearing only beyond localhost
key_concepts.what: Daemon + TLS share one ADR because exposing pharos past loopback is exactly what makes encryption necessary. Today HTTP is localhost-only + plain (Origin-validation guards rebinding, no encryption). Localhost-only = TLS is dead weight.

key_concepts.name: Universal editor bridge (ADR-028, Proposed)
key_concepts.what: v0.3.0+ WebSocket bidirectional protocol; editor plugins push live editor state (open buffers, cursor, focus, selection) so LSP queries reflect unsaved edits. Built from scratch at src/pharos/bridge/ — directory and ADR file do not exist yet.

key_concepts.name: editor_focus() MCP tool (Tier 2)
key_concepts.what: Returns active URI + cursor + selection + viewport + open-file list; lets the LLM ask 'what is the user looking at?' in one call. The single most reusable semantic primitive for an editor integration.

key_concepts.name: Five bridge tiers
key_concepts.what: 1 live document mirroring (mandatory) → 2 editor_focus → 3 diff-preview UX (reverse-channel showDiff into apply_workspace_edit) → 4 diagnostics into native Problems panel → 5 progress into native progress UI.

key_concepts.name: Plugin-per-repo, no build coupling
key_concepts.what: pharos-<editor> repos (pharos-vscode reference, ~200 LOC TS). Pharos owns the versioned spec doc/bridge-protocol.md + bin/test-plugin-conformance.*; plugins implement a JSON contract in their host language.

key_concepts.name: In-VM BEAM message passing (geex advantage)
key_concepts.what: geex is an Elixir OTP app; pharos is Gleam-on-BEAM. Co-located on one VM, geex can send didOpen/didChange/focus as native Erlang terms to the shared LSP pool — no JSON, no WebSocket, no handshake, no TLS, no plugin/conformance stack.

geex_relevance.what_to_take: Take the bridge's SEMANTIC CONTRACT, not its transport. The valuable, reusable artifacts are: (1) the set of editor-state messages — didOpen/didChange/didSave/didClose live-document mirroring (Tier 1, the mandatory core); (2) the editor_focus shape (active URI + cursor + selection + viewport + open-file list); (3) the reverse-channel verbs (showDiff for human-in-loop refactor accept/commit, diagnostics push, progress push). What to SKIP for geex's own pharos integration: the WebSocket server, handshake, capability negotiation, the versioned JSON wire spec, the pharos-<editor> plugin repo, the conformance tester, and TLS. Those exist only to cross an out-of-VM boundary geex does not have. Also worth noting for geex's transport menu generally: the daemon's idle-timeout-instead-of-EOF lifecycle and the well-known-socket auto-discover-or-spawn-ephemeral pattern are clean designs to mirror if geex ever exposes its own services to out-of-VM clients.
geex_relevance.how_it_composes: Maps directly onto geex's one-dispatcher-for-human-and-LLM model. The bridge's tiers ARE commands-as-data: didOpen/didChange/editor_focus/showDiff are exactly the kind of editor-state and editor-action messages that, in geex, become entries in the command table dispatched identically whether a human keystroke, a macro DSL step, or an LLM tool call originated them. Because geex is the editor (not a plugin reporting TO an editor), the data flows BOTH directions through the same dispatcher: geex already HOLDS cursor/selection/buffer state as in-VM data, so 'editor_focus' is a local read of geex state rather than a network round-trip, and 'showDiff' is just another command geex renders natively. Transport recommendation that falls out: for geex<->pharos, prefer in-VM BEAM messaging (direct process calls to the shared LSP pool, terms not JSON) — strictly faster and simpler than stdio/unix-socket/HTTP/WS and eliminates the bridge's serialization+TLS+plugin tax. Reserve stdio for spawning pharos as a child MCP process when not co-located, unix socket / HTTP+TLS only for the genuinely-remote-or-separate-VM case, and treat the WebSocket bridge as the model for THIRD-PARTY editors talking to pharos — not for geex itself.

risks_caveats: ADR-028 and src/pharos/bridge/ do NOT exist yet (verified on disk). The bridge is Proposed/v0.3.0+ vaporware; treat its protocol as a design sketch, not a stable contract geex can integrate against today.
Daemon mode and TLS are v0.2.0 (committed direction) but not shipped; current HTTP transport is localhost-only and plain. Do not assume TLS or a daemon socket exists in v0.1.0.

Roadmap line 3 explicitly states it 'reflects current intent, not commitment' and v0.3.0+ items are exploratory ('expect questions and pivots'). Bridge tiers, plugin LOC estimates, and the editor_focus shape may change.

In-VM geex<->pharos coupling assumes co-location on one BEAM node and that pharos exposes (or can be made to expose) an in-VM API to its LSP pool. Pharos is currently architected around MCP transports (stdio/HTTP); a direct in-VM entry point is not a documented public surface — geex may need pharos to add one, or fall back to unix socket / stdio.

Gleam<->Elixir interop on the BEAM works at the term level but Gleam's typed APIs are not ergonomic to call from Elixir without care (opaque types, custom records); 'free message passing' still needs a deliberately-designed boundary module.

Sharing one warm LSP pool between geex (live, unsaved-buffer state) and other MCP clients (disk state) raises a consistency question the bridge's Tier 1 exists to manage: didChange shadow state must not leak into queries that expect on-disk truth. geex would inherit this coordination problem.

The daemon's idle-timeout lifecycle changes the stdin-EOF assumption MCP hosts rely on; if geex spawns pharos it must decide whether it wants persistent-daemon or ephemeral per-session semantics, and the two interact (auto-discovery could attach geex to a daemon shared with other clients).

findings.topic: Distributed Erlang / BEAM RPC as transport for geex's LLM + collaboration integration
findings.summary: Distributed Erlang gives geex a transparent message-passing fabric where a remote process is addressed almost identically to a local one, which makes the collab tagline `{BufferPid, Node@host} ! {insert, Pos, Text}` nearly literal at the transport layer and makes an in-VM or remote-node LLM agent able to call the command dispatcher directly with zero serialization protocol. The key realization: MCP/JSON-RPC is a boundary technology for crossing a process/trust/language gap; when the LLM agent is itself a BEAM process that gap collapses and it should call `Dispatch.run/1` (commands-as-data structs) directly via message passing or `:erpc`. For geex v0.5 the right answer is a hybrid: keep MCP as the external-client contract (claude-code over stdio) but make the internal dispatch path the single source of truth so the MCP server is a thin adapter, not a parallel write path. The dangerous part is that distributed Erlang's trust model is binary: a node that connects with the right cookie can run arbitrary code on you via :rpc/:erpc, so collab peers and third-party remote agents cannot be untrusted nodes; reserve distribution for nodes you own and make the dispatcher the security chokepoint for everyone else. PIDs-as-capabilities is a real in-VM discipline but leaks across the network and across reconnects, so it is not a network security boundary.
findings.how_it_works:
### 1. Distributed Erlang basics relevant here

Distribution transparency is the whole trick: once two nodes are connected, a remote Pid is messaged with the exact same primitives as a local one (`pid ! msg`, `GenServer.call(pid, ...)`). The runtime serializes the term via External Term Format and ships it over a single long-lived TCP connection per node pair. This is why "edit my buffer from your laptop" *feels* like a one-liner.

- `:erpc.call/4,5` (OTP 23+) is the modern remote-call primitive. Spawns a per-call handler on the target node (no single `rex` server bottleneck like legacy `:rpc`), gives clean per-call timeouts, and propagates remote exceptions with their class so a crash on the remote side raises locally instead of returning a silent `{:badrpc, _}`. Standardize on `:erpc.call/5` for "run function F on node N." Legacy `:rpc` (and `:rpc.call/4`) still works and is fine for fire-and-forget / multicall, but `:erpc` has better failure semantics.
- `GenServer.call({name, node}, msg)` and `GenServer.call(remote_pid, msg)` both work transparently. Sending to `{RegisteredName, Node}` resolves the locally-registered name *on that node*. Note the notes' literal `{BufferPid, Node@host} ! ...` is invalid syntax — you `!` a bare remote Pid, or you send to `{RegisteredName, Node}`; you cannot send to a `{Pid, Node}` tuple.
- Process registry across nodes: `:global` gives cluster-wide *locked* unique names with conflict resolution, but on a netsplit-heal it can *kill* one of two processes that claimed the same name — only use it for true singletons. `:pg` (process groups, the modern replacement for `pg2`) is eventually-consistent and partition-tolerant — the right tool for "all editors currently attached to buffer X" or "the pool of available agent processes."
- Node connection + cookie auth: every node has a magic cookie (`~/.erlang.cookie` or `-setcookie`). The handshake is a challenge-response on that shared secret. **That is the entire authentication and authorization story** — there is no per-call permission layer. `Node.connect/1` (Erlang `net_kernel:connect_node/1`) brings up the link on demand; sending to a process on an unconnected node auto-connects first.
- Hidden nodes (`-hidden` or `connect_node` variants): connect point-to-point *without* joining the transitive global mesh and without appearing in the other node's `Node.list/0`. By default connections are transitive — if A connects to B and B is connected to C, A learns about and meshes with C. `-hidden` defeats that auto-meshing. Necessary for security hygiene but not sufficient (still full-trust after the handshake).

### 2. The collab vision — how literal is it?

At the *transport* layer, very literal. Corrected to valid syntax it is: hold a remote `buffer_pid` and do `buffer_pid ! {:insert, pos, text}`, or `send({:buffer_42, :"geex@bob"}, {:insert, pos, text})`. To edit a buffer on another node you need: (1) the nodes connected (cookie + reachable TCP/EPMD or explicit dist port), (2) a way to *find* the remote buffer process — a registered name or a `:pg` lookup, since you won't have the raw Pid a priori, and (3) the buffer's `handle_info`/`handle_cast` to accept the edit message. That's genuinely a weekend for a naive version, as the notes claim.

What breaks is everything *above* transport — and it's the hard part:
- **Consistency.** Position-relative ops like `{insert, Pos, Text}` are not commutative. Two concurrent inserts at overlapping positions diverge: Pos means different things on each replica once the other's edit lands. Raw message-passing gives you delivery, not convergence. You need a CRDT (or OT) — which, per the notes, wants to live on BEAM anyway. The tagline is a transport mental model, not a collab design.
- **Latency.** Synchronous `GenServer.call` on the per-keystroke path is unusable at real RTT (100ms each way wrecks typing). Collab edits must be async + locally optimistic, reconciled by the CRDT. Distribution does nothing to hide latency.
- **Network partition.** The TCP link drops, you get a `:nodedown`. In-flight casts are lost (no built-in redelivery). On heal, both sides have diverged state to reconcile — again the CRDT's job, plus `:global`/`:pg` re-stabilization.
- **Pid staleness across reconnects.** A Pid encodes a node *incarnation*. After the remote node restarts, every old remote Pid is permanently dead; sending to it silently no-ops (it doesn't even error). So you must **never cache a raw remote Pid across a reconnect** — re-resolve via `:pg`/registered name/handshake on every `:nodedown`→`:nodeup`.
- **Big terms.** Shipping a whole buffer as one message head-of-line-blocks the single inter-node TCP connection for everyone. Keep collab messages small (deltas, not snapshots).

### 3. THE key design question — does an in-BEAM LLM agent need MCP at all?

The crux: **MCP/JSON-RPC is boundary technology.** It exists to cross three gaps at once — process boundary (separate OS process), language boundary (the client isn't Elixir), and trust boundary (foreign code you didn't write). JSON is the lingua franca precisely because the two sides share no runtime. An LLM agent that *is a BEAM process* crosses none of those gaps, so JSON-RPC buys it nothing but serialization overhead and a schema it has to round-trip through.

Separate two things the notes conflate slightly: an LLM **always** needs the *JSON schema* of the commands (that's what populates the model's tool-list in its prompt — true even in-VM). It does **not** always need to *invoke* over JSON-RPC. Schema-export (free from the macro DSL) and transport (MCP vs direct call) are independent axes.

The three topologies:

**(a) External process over stdio JSON-RPC (e.g. claude-code).**
- Cost: full JSON-RPC server inside geex, framing/serialization on every call, an OS subprocess + port to manage, schema must be exact and stable, edits cross a process boundary so they re-enter via the MCP adapter.
- Unlocks: works with *any* MCP client today (claude-code, Cursor, third-party agents) with zero geex-specific code on their side; the trust boundary is real (the external agent only ever sends command structs, never runs code in your VM); language-agnostic.
- This is the right shape for *foreign/untrusted* agents and for "bring your own coding assistant."

**(b) In-VM Elixir/Gleam agent calling `Dispatch.run/1` directly.**
- Cost: the agent is your code, in your supervision tree, in your trust domain — a bug or a prompt-injection can do anything your VM can. No isolation unless you add wasmex/restricted modules.
- Unlocks: zero serialization, sub-microsecond dispatch, the agent shares ETS/state directly, it's "just another typist at the minibuffer" *literally* — same process tree, same undo history, same supervision/crash-recovery, same hot-reload. The notes' loop (LLM action == user action, structurally indistinguishable) is most true here. You still feed the model schemas, you just skip the wire.
- This is the right shape for geex's *own first-party in-pane agent*.

**(c) Remote BEAM node over distributed Erlang RPC.**
- Cost: full distributed-Erlang trust cost (see §4) — connecting the node already granted it arbitrary code execution. Network in the path (latency, partitions, Pid staleness). Cookie management/deployment.
- Unlocks: "run the agent / LSP / model glue on a bigger machine" with the *same `Dispatch.run/1` call*, just `:erpc.call(node, Geex.Dispatch, :run, [cmd], timeout)`. Transparent scaling of heavy work off the editor's node. Genuinely valuable — but only for **infrastructure you own**.

**Right answer for v0.5:** hybrid, with one canonical interface. Make `Dispatch.run/1` over commands-as-data structs *the* interface. Then:
- The minibuffer parses text → struct → `Dispatch.run/1`.
- The MCP server (topology a) is a ~20-line adapter: JSON params → `CommandRegistry.lookup().parse()` → `Dispatch.run/1`. Keep it because it's the external contract and the only safe door for untrusted/foreign agents.
- geex's own in-pane agent (topology b) calls `Dispatch.run/1` directly and uses the schema export only to build its prompt tool-list. No JSON-RPC for the first-party agent.
- Topology (c) is the same `Dispatch.run/1` reached via `:erpc`, enabled later, only for owned nodes, only when off-box compute actually matters.

The point: MCP is *an adapter on top of the one interface, not the interface*. That preserves the notes' "one dispatcher, one history" through-line and avoids building MCP as a parallel write path. Don't make the first-party agent talk JSON to its own VM.

### 4. Security — PIDs-as-capabilities and the distribution trust cliff

**PIDs-as-capabilities (notes line 85)** is real but narrow. It gates *who can message a process* — no Pid, no message — which is a genuinely nice in-VM discipline: don't hand the agent/extension the buffer Pid and it cannot poke the buffer except through whatever door you do hand it (ideally only the dispatcher). But: (1) it only gates messaging, not module calls — a process you spawned can still call `File.read/1`, `:os.cmd/1`, open sockets, `Code.eval_string/1`, regardless of which Pids it holds; (2) it is *not* a network boundary — Pids are forgeable/enumerable across the wire, and any connected node can enumerate processes anyway. So treat it as design hygiene, not a sandbox.

**The distribution trust cliff is the headline risk.** Distributed Erlang has *no intra-cluster authorization*. Cookie auth is binary: once a node passes the handshake it is fully trusted and can `:erpc.call(your_node, :erlang, :halt, [])`, `:erpc.call(your_node, Code, :eval_string, [malicious])`, read every ETS table, message every process. There is no "this node may only call Dispatch.run." And connections are transitive by default, so one compromised peer can pull you into a hostile mesh. **Conclusion: never model untrusted collab peers or third-party agents as distributed Erlang nodes.** Distribution is exclusively for infrastructure *you* control.

How to sandbox, in increasing strength:
- **Dispatcher-as-chokepoint (do this regardless).** The dispatcher only executes *known, schema-validated command structs* — an allowlist, never arbitrary code. Route every untrusted party (MCP client, remote human collaborator, sandboxed agent) through it. This is the security payoff hiding inside the commands-as-data design: untrusted parties get capability without code execution.
- **MCP/stdio for foreign agents.** A subprocess speaking JSON can only ever emit command structs; it has no Pids, no node connection, no module access. The process boundary *is* the sandbox. This is why topology (a) is the right answer for untrusted agents even though (b) is faster.
- **Hidden + TLS distribution for owned nodes.** `-hidden` to avoid auto-meshing, `-proto_dist inet_tls` + `-ssl_dist_optfile` for encrypted/cert-pinned dist, strong unique cookies, firewall EPMD. Reduces blast radius; does *not* change the post-handshake full-trust fact.
- **Restricted-module node.** Run extensions/agents on a separate node with a trimmed module set. Defense-in-depth only — BEAM has no robust in-VM code sandbox, and a determined module can often reach more than intended.
- **wasmex (WebAssembly-in-BEAM).** The only strong *in-process* boundary for untrusted code: the guest can call only host-exported functions — no File, no sockets, no `Code.eval`, no arbitrary Pids. Make the narrow host export surface bottom out at `Dispatch.run/1`. This is the Zed-style WASM-extensions-orchestrated-by-BEAM path the notes already flag (line 90), and it composes perfectly with dispatcher-as-chokepoint.
- **OS-level isolation** (separate user, container, seccomp) under any of the above for code that touches the filesystem/network.

key_concepts.name: Distribution transparency
key_concepts.what: A remote Pid is messaged with the same `!`/`GenServer.call` as a local one; the runtime serializes (External Term Format) and ships over the inter-node TCP link. Makes geex's collab tagline nearly literal at the transport layer.

key_concepts.name: :erpc.call/4,5 (OTP 23+)
key_concepts.what: Modern remote-call primitive: per-call handler (no rex bottleneck), clean timeouts, propagates remote exceptions with class. Standardize on this over legacy :rpc for 'run on that node'.

key_concepts.name: :pg vs :global
key_concepts.what: :pg = eventually-consistent, partition-tolerant process groups, right for 'all editors of buffer X' and agent pools. :global = locked cluster-wide names whose netsplit-heal conflict resolution can kill a process, so only for singletons.

key_concepts.name: Commands-as-data IS the universal interface
key_concepts.what: A command is a serializable struct + a Dispatch.run/1 runner, so the dispatcher is the one true entry point. MCP's call_tool is just JSON->struct->Dispatch.run; an in-VM agent skips the JSON entirely.

key_concepts.name: MCP as boundary tech, not internal tech
key_concepts.what: JSON-RPC/MCP exists to cross process+language+trust gaps. An in-BEAM agent crosses none of them and should call Dispatch.run/1 directly. MCP stays the external contract for foreign/untrusted clients.

key_concepts.name: Schema-export need vs transport need
key_concepts.what: An LLM ALWAYS needs the JSON schema of tools for its prompt context (true even in-VM); it does NOT always need to invoke them over JSON-RPC (only across a boundary). Two independent axes.

key_concepts.name: Pid staleness across reconnects
key_concepts.what: A Pid encodes node incarnation; after a remote restart all old Pids are permanently dead and sends silently no-op. Re-resolve remote handles via :pg / handshake on every :nodedown, never cache raw remote Pids.

key_concepts.name: Distributed-Erlang trust cliff
key_concepts.what: Connection equals full trust. Any cookie-authenticated node can run arbitrary code via :erpc/:rpc, halt your VM, read all ETS. Connections are transitive by default. Distribution is only for infrastructure you own.

key_concepts.name: Hidden nodes
key_concepts.what: -hidden connects point-to-point without joining/seeing the transitive mesh. Defeats 'one compromised peer pulls you into a hostile cluster' but is not sufficient (still full-trust after the handshake).

key_concepts.name: wasmex as the real sandbox
key_concepts.what: WebAssembly-in-BEAM: untrusted code runs with only host-exported functions callable, no File/sockets/Code.eval/arbitrary Pids. The strong in-process boundary; the host's narrow export surface bottoms out at Dispatch.run/1.

key_concepts.name: Dispatcher as security chokepoint
key_concepts.what: The dispatcher only executes known, schema-validated command structs, an allowlist never arbitrary code. Route every untrusted party (MCP client, remote human, sandboxed agent) through it; reserve raw RPC for owned nodes.

geex_relevance.what_to_take: Make Dispatch.run/1 over commands-as-data the single canonical interface, and treat MCP/JSON-RPC strictly as a thin external adapter (parse JSON -> struct -> Dispatch.run) rather than the LLM's only path. For geex's own first-party in-pane agent, run it as an in-VM BEAM process that calls Dispatch.run/1 directly and uses schema-export only to populate the model's prompt tool-list, capturing the 'LLM is just another typist' loop literally (same VM, same undo history, same supervision). Standardize remote work on :erpc.call/5 and use :pg (not :global) for collab participant/buffer registries. Treat the collab tagline as transport-only truth and pair it with a CRDT for the consistency model. Crucially: do NOT use distributed Erlang as the transport for untrusted collab peers or third-party agents; its connect-equals-full-trust model gives any peer arbitrary code execution, so reserve distribution for nodes you own (hidden + TLS dist there) and make the dispatcher the security chokepoint for everyone else, with wasmex for untrusted in-VM extension/agent code.
geex_relevance.how_it_composes: Directly extends geex's stated through-line ('one vocabulary, one dispatcher, one history, used by humans and LLMs identically', notes line 377). The commands-as-data + macro-DSL design already makes the dispatcher a serializable, schema-described allowlist, which is simultaneously (1) the universal call interface for human/plugin/in-VM-agent/remote-agent, (2) the natural collab edit-command unit, and (3) the security chokepoint that lets untrusted parties in without granting code execution. MCP becomes one of several thin adapters on top of that one interface rather than a parallel write path, preserving the 'all three for the price of one DSL block' property (line 287) and extending it to a fourth and fifth consumer (in-VM and remote-node agents). It sharpens the notes' line 374 ('AI is just another participant') by separating transport (trivial via distribution), consistency (CRDT), and trust (dispatcher-as-allowlist, not raw RPC).

risks_caveats: The notes' tagline `{BufferPid, Node@host} ! ...` is not valid syntax: you `!` a bare remote Pid, or send to `{RegisteredName, Node}`. Minor but worth correcting in the design doc.

Transport is trivial; CONSISTENCY is the real collab work. Raw position-relative `{insert, Pos, Text}` ops are not commutative and diverge under concurrent edits + latency + partition. A CRDT (or OT) is mandatory; the tagline is a transport mental model, not a collab design.

Distributed Erlang has NO intra-cluster authorization: cookie auth equals full trust equals arbitrary code execution via :rpc/:erpc, plus transitive auto-meshing. NEVER model untrusted collab peers or third-party agents as distributed nodes. This is the single biggest trap in the whole analysis.

PIDs-as-capabilities only gates messaging, not module calls (File, :os.cmd, Code.eval, sockets remain callable), and is not a network boundary (Pids are forgeable/enumerable across the wire). It is a design discipline, not a sandbox.
Synchronous GenServer.call on the per-keystroke remote path is unusable at real RTT (e.g. 100ms). Collab edits must be async + locally optimistic, reconciled by the CRDT.
Remote Pids go permanently dead across a node restart and sends silently no-op; caching raw remote Pids across reconnects is a latent bug. Re-resolve via :pg/handshake on every :nodedown.
A single huge message (e.g. shipping a whole buffer) head-of-line-blocks the single TCP inter-node connection. Avoid giant terms on the collab/agent link.
:global's netsplit-heal conflict resolution can kill a registered process; prefer :pg for anything that is not a strict singleton.
BEAM has no robust in-VM code sandbox; a restricted-module node is defense-in-depth, not a real boundary. wasmex or OS-level isolation are the only strong sandboxes for untrusted code.

Topology (c) is genuinely valuable (agent/LSP on a bigger machine) but only for infrastructure you own; its security cost is total, so do not reach for it as the general external-agent answer; that is topology (a)/MCP.

findings.topic: Jido (agentjido/jido) — Elixir autonomous-agent framework: architecture, Actions/Agents/Signals/Sensors, schema validation, MCP/LLM tool export, and comparison to geex's "commands as data"
findings.summary: Jido is an Elixir framework for building autonomous, distributed, fault-tolerant agents on OTP. Its core unit, an Action, is structurally close to geex's planned command: a module that does `use Jido.Action` with a `name`/`description`/`schema`, a required `run(params, context)` callback returning `{:ok, result}` | `{:ok, result, directives}` | `{:error, reason}`, automatic NimbleOptions (or Zoi) validation, automatic JSON-Schema generation, and a `to_tool/0` that emits an LLM tool definition. Jido v2 is split into packages — `jido` (agent runtime), `jido_action` (Action + Exec executor + Instruction), `jido_signal` (CloudEvents v1.0.2 signals + trie router), `jido_ai` (ReqLLM-based ReAct loop), and critically `jido_mcp` which BOTH consumes external MCP servers AND exposes Jido Actions as MCP tools via `use Jido.MCP.Server`. This is almost exactly the architecture geex's notes.md describes wanting to hand-roll (macro DSL -> struct + run + JSON schema -> uniform dispatch by human/plugin/LLM -> MCP export). The decisive divergence: Jido is an agent-runtime (its "state" is an agent's mind, its execution model is signal-routed autonomous behavior with retries/async/supervision), whereas geex commands are synchronous editor operations against editor state where undo/replay/collab determinism matter more than autonomy — and Jido's Action is a module+behavior, not a value-struct of the args, which slightly cuts against geex's "command IS the value" requirement.
findings.how_it_works:
PACKAGE LAYOUT (v2): Jido is no longer one library. `jido_action` holds Jido.Action, Jido.Exec (executor), Jido.Instruction (normalization). `jido_signal` holds Jido.Signal + Jido.Signal.Router. `jido` holds Jido.Agent + the OTP server (Jido.Agent.Server / AgentServer) + Sensors. `jido_ai` is the LLM layer (ReqLLM). `jido_mcp` is MCP client+server. Geex would depend on `jido_action` and maybe `jido_mcp` — NOT the whole agent stack.

ACTION (jido_action): An Action is an Elixir MODULE, not a plain struct of args. `use Jido.Action, name: "...", description: "...", category:, tags:, vsn:, schema: [..], output_schema: [..], compensation: [..]`. The macro validates the config at compile time and exposes metadata via generated functions (name/0, schema/0, to_json/0, to_tool/0). The only required callback is `run(params, context)` where `params` is the already-validated map and `context` is a side-channel map; returns `{:ok, map}` | `{:ok, map, directives}` | `{:error, reason}`. Optional lifecycle hooks: on_before_validate_params/1, on_after_validate_params/1, on_before_validate_output/1, on_after_validate_output/1, on_after_run/1, on_error/4 (compensation). There IS a `Jido.Action.t()` metadata type (name/description/category/tags/vsn/schema/output_schema), but the args you pass at call time travel as a plain validated `map`, not as a `%MyAction{}` struct value — i.e. Jido does not `defstruct` the action's arguments the way geex's "%Command.Copy{range:..}" design does.

EXECUTION (Jido.Exec): `Jido.Exec.run(action_module, params, context, opts)` runs synchronously with validation, automatic retries with exponential backoff, timeout handling, process monitoring, telemetry. `Jido.Exec.run_async/2` spawns under a Task.Supervisor (mailbox-bound to caller); `Jido.Exec.await(ref, timeout)`. `Jido.Instruction.normalize/2` turns `MyAction` | `{MyAction, params}` | `%Instruction{}` | lists into uniform `%Jido.Instruction{action, params, context, opts}` structs — this normalization is the closest thing to geex's "parser produces command values; dispatcher runs them." Chaining: each action's output map merges into the next action's params ("open validation" — unknown keys pass through), enabling pipelines.

AGENT: `use Jido.Agent, name:, description:, schema: [..]` (state schema, NimbleOptions or Zoi). The agent is an IMMUTABLE STRUCT `Jido.Agent.t()` (state map + id/name/metadata + agent_module + schema), explicitly NOT a GenServer. Functions: `new/0,1`, `set/2` (merge+validate state), `validate/2`, and `cmd(agent, instructions) -> {agent, directives}`. Key design: cmd returns a fully-updated agent (no separate "apply directives" step) plus a list of DIRECTIVES — bare structs describing effects for the runtime to interpret (%Directive.Emit{}, .Spawn{}, .Schedule{}, .RunInstruction{}, .StartSensor{}, .Stop{}). Directives never mutate state; state changes are in the returned agent. This is an Elm/Redux split: pure decision (agent struct) vs runtime-owned effects (directives). OTP wrapping is a separate Jido.Agent.Server/AgentServer GenServer.

SIGNALS (jido_signal): CloudEvents v1.0.2-compliant envelope. Fields: specversion ("1.0.2"), id (UUID v7, monotonic), source ("/auth/registration"), type (dot notation e.g. "user.profile.updated"), plus optional subject/time/datacontenttype/dataschema/data. Routed by a trie-based Jido.Signal.Router with exact ("user.created"), single-wildcard ("user.*.updated"), and multi-wildcard ("audit.**") matches; routes map type-string -> Action module, e.g. `{"chat.message", MyApp.Actions.HandleMessage}`. Priority layers: strategy(50+)/agent(0)/plugin(-10). Fallback: treat {type, data} as the instruction. signal_routes are declared on the agent.

SENSORS: A GenServer (wrapped by Jido.Sensor.Runtime) that watches an external source (PubSub, webhook, queue, DB change, timer) and emits typed Signals into the agent. `use Jido.Sensor, name:, description:, schema:` with callbacks init/2, handle_event/2, terminate/2. Started via supervision/StartSensor directive with `context: %{agent_ref: ...}`; connected AgentServer routes emitted signals to matching actions. Sensor crashes emit a `jido.agent.sensor.exit` signal.

VALIDATION: Schemas are NimbleOptions (keyword-list, traditional) OR Zoi (recommended for transforms/refinements/nested). Validation is RUNTIME (at Jido.Exec.run / agent set), via a Jido.Action.Schema adapter that detects schema type. "Open" semantics — only declared fields are validated; extras pass through (enables chaining). `Jido.Action.Schema.to_json_schema/1` converts schema -> JSON Schema; `to_tool/0` emits strict schemas (recursive additionalProperties:false). Mapping: type->"type", required:true-> "required" array, :doc/description-> "description", {:in,[..]}/enum-> "enum".

LLM/MCP: `MyAction.to_tool/0` returns %{name, description, function, parameters_schema: %{"type"=>"object","properties"=>..,"required"=>..}} (LangChain/ReqLLM-compatible). jido_ai exposes Actions to an LLM via `Jido.AI.Agent` with a `tools: [Actions...]` param and a ReAct loop (ask_sync/3, ask/3+await/2, allowed_tools:/tool_context: gating), backed by ReqLLM (Anthropic/OpenAI/Google). jido_mcp is bidirectional: CLIENT (Jido.MCP.list_tools/call_tool/read_resource over {:stdio|:sse|:streamable_http}, built on anubis_mcp) and SERVER — `use Jido.MCP.Server, name:, version:, publish: %{tools: [..Actions], resources: [..], prompts: [..]}` with explicit allowlist publication, served over Anubis.Server.Transport.StreamableHTTP.Plug. This server side is precisely geex's "the editor IS an MCP server, every command is a tool" goal, already implemented.

key_concepts.name: Action (module + behavior, not arg-struct)
key_concepts.what: `use Jido.Action, name:, description:, schema:` defines a module with a required `run(params, context)` returning {:ok,map}|{:ok,map,directives}|{:error,reason}. Metadata via name/0, schema/0, to_json/0, to_tool/0. Validated params arrive as a plain map - Jido does NOT defstruct the arguments (the divergence from geex's command-as-value).

key_concepts.name: Jido.Exec (executor)
key_concepts.what: Runs an action: Jido.Exec.run(mod, params, ctx, opts) sync with NimbleOptions/Zoi validation, retries+exponential backoff, timeouts, monitoring, telemetry; run_async/2 + await/2 for async under Task.Supervisor. The 'runner' analogous to geex's run(struct,state) but with autonomy/reliability machinery layered on.

key_concepts.name: Jido.Instruction (normalization/dispatch)
key_concepts.what: normalize/2 turns Module | {Module,params} | %Instruction{} | lists into uniform %Jido.Instruction{action,params,context,opts}. Closest analog to geex's 'parser produces values, dispatcher runs them.'

key_concepts.name: Agent = immutable struct + cmd/2 -> {agent, directives}
key_concepts.what: Pure functional Elm/Redux split: cmd returns a fully-updated agent plus a list of effect directives (Emit/Spawn/Schedule/RunInstruction/Stop). Directives never mutate state. OTP wrapping (Jido.Agent.Server) is separate. Geex's editor state is closer to a single mutable session, not per-action immutable agent minds.

key_concepts.name: Signal (CloudEvents v1.0.2) + trie Router
key_concepts.what: Standardized event envelope (specversion/id/source/type/data) routed by Jido.Signal.Router with exact + '*'/'**' wildcard type matching to Action modules. Lives in jido_signal. Geex editor ops are synchronous local dispatch, not event-routed - likely overkill for the command layer.

key_concepts.name: Sensor (GenServer -> emits Signals)
key_concepts.what: use Jido.Sensor with init/2, handle_event/2, terminate/2; wrapped by Jido.Sensor.Runtime; watches external sources and feeds Signals to agents. Agent-runtime concept; no direct geex command-system analog.

key_concepts.name: to_tool/0 + JSON Schema generation
key_concepts.what: Action.to_tool/0 emits %{name, description, function, parameters_schema(JSON Schema)} from the NimbleOptions schema (type/required/doc/enum mapping), strict (additionalProperties:false). This is EXACTLY geex's 'macro generates JSON schema -> free LLM tool' payoff, already built.

key_concepts.name: jido_mcp (bidirectional MCP)
key_concepts.what: CLIENT: Jido.MCP.list_tools/call_tool/read_resource over stdio/sse/streamable_http (on anubis_mcp). SERVER: `use Jido.MCP.Server, publish: %{tools:, resources:, prompts:}` allowlist, served via Anubis StreamableHTTP plug. The server side = geex's 'editor IS an MCP server' goal already implemented.

key_concepts.name: Open validation semantics
key_concepts.what: Only declared schema fields are validated; extra fields pass through unchanged, so action outputs merge into the next action's params for chaining. Useful for pipelines; geex commands probably want stricter closed validation for editor correctness.

geex_relevance.what_to_take: Take the jido_action sub-package's proven design as a blueprint and seriously evaluate depending on it directly for the COMMAND-DEFINITION + SCHEMA + LLM-TOOL-EXPORT slice - do NOT pull in the full agent/signal/sensor runtime. The three things Jido already solved that geex's notes.md plans to hand-roll: (1) `use Jido.Action` macro DSL with name/description/schema -> compile-time-checked metadata; (2) NimbleOptions schema -> automatic JSON Schema via to_json_schema/1 and an LLM tool via to_tool/0 (strict, additionalProperties:false); (3) jido_mcp's `use Jido.MCP.Server, publish: %{tools: [...]}` which is LITERALLY geex's 'the editor IS an MCP server, every command is a tool' goal, already built on anubis_mcp with stdio/SSE/HTTP transports. Adopting jido_action + jido_mcp could delete the entire 'macro DSL -> schema -> MCP export' chunk of geex's roadmap (notes.md lines 201-388). Reference Jido.Instruction.normalize and Jido.Exec as the model for geex's parser->dispatcher and runner. The one piece to ADAPT rather than adopt verbatim: geex wants the command to be a VALUE (%Command.Copy{} struct) for undo/replay/macro-recording/serialization, while Jido passes validated maps to run(params,ctx) and reserves structs for agent state/instructions - geex can either wrap each command's params in its own struct on top of a Jido.Action module, or generate both, but should not abandon the command-as-value property since undo/replay/collab determinism is geex's whole point.
geex_relevance.how_it_composes: Geex's three pillars map cleanly onto Jido: (a) commands-as-data == Jido.Instruction (a normalized {action, params, context} value the dispatcher runs) - but geex must keep the params as a typed struct, not Jido's open map, to get deterministic undo/replay/serialization; (b) macro DSL generating struct+run+JSON-schema == `use Jido.Action` + NimbleOptions + to_tool/0 essentially 1:1; (c) one dispatcher for human/plugin/LLM == Jido.Exec.run as the runner + jido_mcp.Server as the LLM/external surface + the same Action callable from minibuffer parse, plugin code, and MCP tool call. WHERE THEY DIVERGE AND WHY IT MATTERS: Jido is an autonomous-agent runtime - its execution model centers on Signals (CloudEvents event-routing), Sensors (GenServers watching the outside world), Directives (deferred effects), retries/timeouts/async, and per-agent immutable 'minds'. Geex commands are SYNCHRONOUS, LOCAL editor operations against one editing session where the prized properties are determinism, undo history, replay, and collab-CRDT integration - not autonomy, retries, or event routing. So the Signal/Router/Sensor/Directive/Agent half of Jido is wrong-shaped weight for an editor command bus (geex's dispatch is 'parse -> lookup -> run(struct,state) -> record for undo', not 'route CloudEvent -> agent decides -> emit directives'). NET: adopt the Action/schema/tool/MCP slice (it is the framework geex would otherwise hand-roll, and hand-rolling JSON-Schema generation + an MCP server is weeks of work jido_action+jido_mcp already shipped), but keep geex's own thin command-as-value struct + synchronous editor-state dispatcher on top, and skip the agent-runtime layers. Caveat the dependency cost: jido_action pulls NimbleOptions/Zoi (fine, tiny) and jido_mcp pulls anubis_mcp + a Plug/HTTP stack (heavier - acceptable since geex already wants an MCP server, but verify it can run over stdio without forcing Phoenix/Plug if geex stays a pure TUI binary).

risks_caveats: Jido v2 had a recent major rewrite (Show HN: 'Jido 2.0') and split into many packages (jido, jido_action, jido_signal, jido_ai, jido_mcp); APIs are young and may churn - pin versions and expect breaking changes. As of the docs seen: jido v2.2-2.3, jido_action v2.2.1, jido_ai v2.1.

Structural mismatch on the core property geex cares about: Jido.Action passes a validated MAP to run(params, context); it does NOT defstruct the action's arguments. Geex's 'command IS the value' (%Command.Copy{}) for undo/replay/macro-recording/serialization is therefore NOT what Jido gives out of the box - geex must wrap or generate its own arg-structs on top. Don't assume adopting Jido gets you command-as-value for free.

Jido uses 'open' validation (extra/unknown params pass through) to enable action chaining. For an editor command system you likely want CLOSED/strict validation so a malformed/typo'd command from an LLM or plugin is rejected, not silently accepted - you'd need to override or wrap this.

jido_mcp server depends on anubis_mcp and is documented with a Plug/StreamableHTTP transport; confirm it supports a pure stdio MCP server without dragging in Phoenix/Plug, since geex aims to be a small single-binary (Burrito) TUI. The HTTP transport may be unwanted weight.

Pulling the FULL jido (agent + signal + sensor + directives) into an editor would import an autonomous-agent paradigm geex doesn't need; the value is concentrated in jido_action (+ optionally jido_mcp), so depend narrowly rather than on the umbrella.

Some specifics here were synthesized from docs/READMEs via WebFetch summaries rather than reading source; before committing, verify against the actual jido_action source (to_tool/0 exact shape, whether run/2 params is map vs struct, whether closed validation is configurable) and the jido_mcp transport options.

Adopting an external framework conflicts with geex's stated 'leverage Elixir macros / hand-roll the DSL' ethos (notes.md) and adds an upstream dependency on a small-team project; weigh ecosystem-leverage vs control/longevity for something as central as the command bus.

findings.topic: BalanceBeam — "LLM-Aware Library Design for the BEAM" (an "Ecto for LLMs" sketch, revised into a production trust layer over instructor_ex + Jido)
findings.summary: BalanceBeam is a design-research repo (no implementation; the .exs is explicitly "a SPEC, not an implementation") sketching a typed, supervised, schema-driven Elixir library for LLM-mediated workflows. It contains TWO designs in tension. The ORIGINAL thesis (README + Phase 2): one schema definition drives prompts + validation + types ("type-driven prompts," Strategy 4), LLM calls made visible in signatures via effect typing (Strategy 2: ~llm ~retry ~validate), and OTP-supervised execution of nondeterministic calls (Strategy 5) — pitched as "Ecto for LLMs." The REVISED design (phase_1_foundation.md, after an ecosystem audit) explicitly retracts that: schema-driven extraction is already shipped by instructor_ex and agent supervision by Jido, so rebuilding them is "the failure mode of yet another LLM library." BalanceBeam is rescoped to "the production trust layer" — four wedge features (Replay, Cost budgets+fallback, Provenance, Trust boundaries+PHI redaction) wired declaratively over instructor_ex/Jido/req_llm via a compile-time @bb_effects annotation. For geex this is highly relevant: BalanceBeam's revised position (be the cross-cutting trust/audit/provenance wrapper, delegate schema+execution to existing tools) is exactly the role geex needs for its LLM loop, and its bb_trust/bb_redact (Strategy 10) and provenance (Strategy 9/19) primitives map directly onto geex's "every AI edit is an audited struct in undo history."
findings.how_it_works:
ARCHITECTURE (revised, Elixir-only v0.1): A three-layer stack expressed as a single mix project. (1) MACRO/SCHEMA LAYER — `defschema`-style macros plus the bb_* declarations; the key generated artifacts per the diagram are "Schema → struct + validator", "Schema → JSON schema", "Schema → prompt fragments", "Effect annotations → wrappers". (2) RUNTIME LAYER (plain OTP) — per-call DynamicSupervisor, retry handler, fallback chain, ETS-backed cost ledger, telemetry, cassette record/replay, and a Model Adapter behaviour (Claude/OpenAI/Local). (3) BEAM. The polyglot doc is the aspirational future: Elixir for macros, Gleam for typed orchestration/message protocols/trust types, Erlang for low-level primitives (pools, rate limiters, circuit breakers, cost ledgers), with bytecode-level FFI; explicitly NOT the starting point.

THE REVISION (load-bearing). phase_1_foundation.md opens with a "Note on revision" that retracts the original trio as Phase 1. Rationale: (a) instructor_ex already does schema-driven extraction (Ecto.Schema + @llm_doc + JSON-schema emission); (b) the Jido ecosystem (jido_ai, jido_action, req_llm, jido_signal) already does agent supervision, tool calling, ReAct loops; (c) effect typing "as a visible-in-signatures feature does not pay off in dynamic Elixir" — the Dialyzer story is shaky and a custom analysis pass is heavy infra for marginal value; that pitch "loses to a typed BEAM language whenever effect typing genuinely matters." So the new identity is "the production trust layer for Elixir LLM applications. Replay, cost, trust, and provenance — declaratively wired via effect annotations — over whatever combination of instructor_ex, jido, and req_llm the user has assembled."

EFFECT ANNOTATIONS AS WIRING SPINE. The original `~llm ~retry ~validate(Schema)` markers are reframed from "visible nondeterminism" (kept only as documentation) into a COMPILE-TIME WRAPPER INSTALLATION MECHANISM. A user writes once: `@bb_effects [:llm, :validate, :tool_call, :budget, :provenance]` above `def review(pdf_bytes, plan_id)`, and each tag mechanically triggers a specific wrapper: :llm → telemetry+cost accumulation+cassette recording; :validate → retry-on-validation-error policy; :tool_call → tool calls become provenance entries with cost attribution; :budget → bb_budget enforcement active for the function scope; :provenance → return value wrapped with __provenance__ metadata. No per-call wiring; "the effect list is mechanically meaningful — each tag triggers a specific wrapper — not just documentation."

TARGET API DATA MODEL (v01_target_api.exs, three tiers). Tier 1 = an unchanged instructor_ex schema (Ecto embedded_schema + @llm_doc docstring + validate_changeset/1). Tier 2 = unchanged Jido.Action tool modules (name/description/schema + run/2) and an unchanged Jido.AI.Agent (strategy: :react, model: {:anthropic, "claude-sonnet-4-6"}, tools: [...], system_prompt). Tier 3 = the BalanceBeam.Pipeline module, which is the only thing v0.1 must implement. Inside it: `use BalanceBeam.Pipeline` installs the macro env; module-level declarations `bb_redact SchemaMod, field: :policy`, `bb_trust SchemaMod, field: :untrusted`, `bb_budget max_cost: 0.50, currency: :usd, on_exceed: :escalate_to_human`; then the `@bb_effects [...]` function. The function body composes runtime calls in a `with`: `BalanceBeam.replay_or_record :prior_auth, {pdf_bytes, plan_id} do ... end` wraps the block; inside, `BalanceBeam.extract(SchemaMod, text)` (thin wrapper over Instructor.chat_completion/1 adding cassette/cost/provenance/redaction/trust-wrapping), `BalanceBeam.supervise(reviewer, Mod, :run, [reviewer, request])` (runs the Jido agent under a per-request DynamicSupervisor, intercepting calls via Jido telemetry hooks; on crash restarts once with accumulated state, on second crash returns {:error, :agent_crashed, partial_provenance}), and finally `BalanceBeam.attach_provenance(decision)`.

RETURN/PROVENANCE SHAPE. Success returns {:ok, %Decision{verdict: :approve, reasoning: ..., cited_policy_version: ..., __provenance__: %BalanceBeam.Provenance{request_id, cassette_id, total_cost_cents, steps: [%{step: :extract, schema: ..., model: ..., cost_cents: 4, retries: 0, cassette_segment: "ext_001"}, %{step: :tool_call, tool: ..., cassette_segment: "tool_001"}, ..., %{step: :llm_decision, model: ..., cost_cents: 19, cassette_segment: "dec_001"}]}}}. Failure tuples ALWAYS carry partial provenance: {:error, :budget_exceeded, partial_provenance}, {:error, :extraction_failed, changeset, partial_provenance}, {:error, :agent_crashed, partial_provenance}, {:error, :validation_exhausted_retries, last_attempt, partial_provenance}. "There is no failure path that loses provenance." Replay makes CI deterministic and free (same source runs in record vs replay mode controlled only by Mix.env() == :test or Application config).

TRUST/REDACTION MECHANICS (Strategy 10/22 + 17). bb_trust marks fields :untrusted; at compile time they are wrapped in BalanceBeam.Untrusted.t(); any path that interpolates a wrapped value into a prompt string, tool argument, or system message fails to compile (or fails at runtime in the dynamic tier). The ONLY legal extraction is BalanceBeam.delimit_isolate/1, which wraps content in delimiters the model is instructed to treat as user data. bb_redact declares schema-level PHI policies (:pseudonymize | :hash | :remove | :keep); when the runtime is about to call an adapter whose trust_level/0 returns :external, listed fields are transformed outbound, the pseudonym table is stored per-request (lives only for the request) and recorded in the cassette, and originals are restored on the inbound side. Local-model calls skip redaction (inside the trust boundary).

key_concepts.name: Type-driven prompts (Strategy 4, original thesis)
key_concepts.what: One schema definition drives prompts + validation + types simultaneously. The macro layer compiles a schema into: struct + validator, JSON schema, prompt fragments, and effect-aware wrappers — all four from one declaration. This is the 'Ecto for LLMs' core. NOTE the revision: BalanceBeam now DELEGATES schema definition to instructor_ex (Ecto.Schema + @llm_doc) rather than building its own defschema; the remaining open gap it might still own is model-specific prompt synthesis (XML tags for Claude vs function-calling JSON for GPT) via a BalanceBeam.prompt_for/2 macro.

key_concepts.name: Effect typing (Strategy 2) — reframed
key_concepts.what: Original: ~llm ~retry ~validate(Schema) markers make LLM nondeterminism visible in function signatures, propagating to callers. Revised verdict: 'does not pay off in dynamic Elixir' as a type feature; survives ONLY as documentation. The MECHANISM survives as @bb_effects [:llm, :validate, :tool_call, :budget, :provenance] — a compile-time declaration that mechanically installs production wrappers. This is the single 'wiring spine' that ties all four wedge features together with no per-call boilerplate.

key_concepts.name: Supervised execution (Strategy 5)
key_concepts.what: OTP supervision applied to model nondeterminism. BalanceBeam.supervise/4 runs a (Jido) agent under a per-request DynamicSupervisor; LLM/tool calls are intercepted via telemetry; crash → restart once with accumulated state → second crash returns {:error, :agent_crashed, partial_provenance}. Retry/fallback are supervisor-scoped policies. Revised design delegates the agent runtime itself to Jido and only wraps it.

key_concepts.name: Four wedge features (revised Phase 1)
key_concepts.what: Replay (Strategy 20): append-only cassette of every LLM+tool call indexed by request ID; record in prod, replay deterministically in CI. Cost budgets+fallback (Strategy 12): bb_budget per-request ceiling with on_exceed policy (:error | :escalate_to_human | {:fallback, model_id}). Provenance (Strategy 19): __provenance__ value-level metadata of every step (model, prompt version, cassette segment, cost, retries, fallbacks, nested tool calls). Trust boundaries+PHI redaction (Strategies 22+17): bb_trust Untrusted wrapper + bb_redact pseudonymize/hash/remove/keep. All four share the @bb_effects wiring mechanism.

key_concepts.name: Replay/cassette as substrate
key_concepts.what: BalanceBeam.replay_or_record/2 wraps a pipeline; cassettes capture prompts, responses, tool I/O, model IDs, prompt versions, latencies, cost. Doubles as the foundation for the eval framework and semantic cache. Cassettes are versioned so future replays can detect divergence. This is what makes LLM systems testable at all (vs slow/nondeterministic real calls or behavior-decoupled mocks).

key_concepts.name: Provenance (Strategy 9/19)
key_concepts.what: Every value carries __provenance__ recording origin (module/function/line), model+version, prompt/schema version, cassette segment, cost in cents, retries, fallbacks, nested tool-call entries, timestamps. Stronger than external APM because it tags the DATA FLOW between calls, not just the calls. Every error path also carries partial provenance — no path loses it. Also the foundation for eval, fine-tuning data curation, and observability dashboards.

key_concepts.name: Trust boundaries (Strategy 10/22)
key_concepts.what: Trusted.t() vs Untrusted.t() type distinction prevents untrusted prompt content from being concatenated into trusted positions without explicit, auditable wrapping. delimit_isolate/1 is the only sanctioned promotion; unsafe_promote_to_trusted() is the auditable escape hatch. bb_trust declares it per schema field. Strongest differentiator for regulated/sensitive-data buyers; a real (typed) defense against prompt injection rather than 'asking the model nicely.'

key_concepts.name: Three-tier delegation model
key_concepts.what: Tier 1 instructor_ex schemas (unchanged), Tier 2 Jido actions + agents (unchanged), Tier 3 BalanceBeam.Pipeline (the only new code). The library's discipline: 'BalanceBeam does not redefine schemas / does not redefine tools'; it wraps. This is the architecturally important stance for any consumer deciding how to layer it.

geex_relevance.what_to_take: Take BalanceBeam's REVISED architectural stance and its two security/audit primitives; do NOT take the original 'Ecto for LLMs' trio wholesale (the author himself retracted it). Specifically: (1) The convergence thesis is real and strong. geex's macro DSL already generates JSON schemas from command declarations; BalanceBeam generates 'struct + validator + JSON schema + prompt fragments' from ONE schema. These are the same compile-time artifact pipeline. geex command schemas CAN double as BalanceBeam-style LLM operation schemas: when the LLM calls a geex command as a tool, the JSON schema geex already emits is exactly what an instructor_ex/structured-output validator needs, and BalanceBeam's :validate effect (retry-on-validation-error) is precisely the loop geex would want around a tool call that fails its own schema. geex already has the 'one declaration → schema' half; BalanceBeam adds the 'schema → validated/retried/recorded LLM call' half. (2) The @bb_effects compile-time-wrapper pattern is the single most reusable idea for geex: a per-command/per-operation effect list ([:llm, :validate, :provenance, :tool_call]) that mechanically installs wrappers maps cleanly onto geex's 'one dispatcher for human and LLM' — the same command, dispatched by a human, skips :llm but keeps :provenance; dispatched by an LLM, adds :validate/:tool_call. (3) Strategy 10 (bb_trust/Untrusted + delimit_isolate) and Strategy 9/19 (provenance struct + 'no failure path loses provenance') are DIRECTLY the machinery for geex's 'every AI edit is an audited struct in undo history.' A geex edit command, when LLM-originated, should be wrapped exactly like BalanceBeam wraps extract: the resulting command struct gets a __provenance__ field (model, prompt version, cassette segment, cost, retries) and its string args sourced from model output are Untrusted.t() until delimit_isolate'd. That makes undo-history entries audit-grade for free.
geex_relevance.how_it_composes: geex is commands-as-data + a macro DSL that emits JSON schemas + one dispatcher for both human and LLM callers. BalanceBeam is the missing AI-layer that sits AROUND that dispatcher when the caller is an LLM. The clean composition: geex's command struct IS BalanceBeam's 'operation'; geex's generated JSON schema IS the structured-output contract BalanceBeam validates against; geex's dispatcher is what BalanceBeam.supervise/replay_or_record wraps. Because geex commands are already data structs, attaching __provenance__ to them and recording them to a cassette is trivial — they are the same audited-struct that already lives in undo history, so 'provenance' and 'undo entry' become the same object. The @bb_effects annotation could be a per-command attribute in geex's DSL ('this command, when LLM-dispatched, runs under [:validate, :provenance, :budget]'), making the human-vs-LLM dispatch difference declarative rather than branch logic. IS BalanceBeam the AI-layer geex should build its LLM loop on? Conceptually YES — its revised identity (be the trust/audit/provenance/replay wrapper, delegate schema+execution downward) is exactly the layer geex needs, and the primitives map 1:1. PRACTICALLY: BalanceBeam is an unbuilt design sketch (no code; .exs is a SPEC), is Elixir-and-Jido/instructor_ex-specific, and assumes Ecto schemas rather than geex's own command DSL. So geex should ADOPT THE DESIGN (effect-annotation wiring spine, provenance struct shape, Untrusted/delimit_isolate trust model, replay-cassette-for-deterministic-tests, partial-provenance-on-every-error invariant) but implement it natively against geex command structs rather than depend on BalanceBeam or pull in the instructor_ex/Jido stack it wraps. The convergence is at the design level; the dependency would be premature.

findings.topic: instructor_ex: Ecto-schema-driven structured LLM outputs in Elixir — and its applicability to geex's command validation boundary
findings.summary: instructor_ex (a port of Python's `instructor`) extracts validated, structured data from LLMs in Elixir. You define an Ecto `embedded_schema` annotated with an `@llm_doc` description and an optional `validate_changeset/1` callback, then call `Instructor.chat_completion(model:, response_model:, max_retries:, messages:)` and get back `{:ok, %YourStruct{}}` or `{:error, %Ecto.Changeset{}}`. Under the hood it derives a JSON Schema from the Ecto schema, ships it to the LLM via tool-calling / json / md_json modes, casts the LLM's JSON back through an Ecto changeset, runs your validations, and on failure feeds the formatted changeset errors back to the model (`max_retries`) for an automatic reask loop. It is model-agnostic via an `Instructor.Adapter` behaviour with adapters for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Ollama, llamacpp, Groq, vLLM, and xAI. For geex this is precisely the "JSON Schema in, validated struct out, with retries" boundary that sits on both sides of MCP — but the two directions (geex calling an LLM vs an LLM calling geex tools) want different parts of it.
findings.how_it_works:
ARCHITECTURE / CONTROL FLOW. The public entry point is `Instructor.chat_completion/1,2` with `@spec chat_completion([Keyword.t], [any]) :: {:ok, Ecto.Schema.t} | {:error, Ecto.Changeset.t} | {:error, String.t} | stream`. Options: `:model`, `:response_model` (an Ecto schema module, or a bare map of `field => Ecto.Type` for ad-hoc schemas, or wrappers like `{:array, Schema}` / `{:partial, Schema}`), `:messages`, `:adapter` (default `Instructor.Adapters.OpenAI`), `:max_retries` (default 0), `:mode` (`:tools` default, `:json`, `:md_json`), and `:validation_context` (default `%{}`).

The internal `do_chat_completion/3` loop is the heart: (1) it derives a JSON Schema from `response_model` and injects it into the request — in `:tools` mode as an OpenAI/Anthropic function/tool definition, in `:json` mode as a `response_format`/json-schema, in `:md_json` mode as a prompt-embedded schema for models without native structured output; (2) calls the adapter's `chat_completion/2`; (3) takes the raw JSON the model produced and runs `cast_all/2` — for an Ecto schema this pulls fields, embeds and associations, does `Ecto.Changeset.cast(params, fields)`, applies custom Ecto type overrides, and recursively casts embeds/associations; (4) runs `call_validate/3`, which dispatches to `response_model.validate_changeset/1` or `/2` (with context) if exported, else returns the changeset unchanged; (5) if the changeset is valid, returns `{:ok, struct}` via `apply_changes`; (6) if invalid AND `max_retries > 0`, it formats the errors with `Instructor.ErrorFormatter.format_errors(changeset)`, decrements `max_retries`, appends `reask_messages(...)` plus a system message like "...fix the following validation errors:\n#{errors}" to the conversation, and recurses; (7) when retries are exhausted it returns `{:error, changeset}`.

ADAPTER ABSTRACTION. `Instructor.Adapter` is a behaviour with `@callback chat_completion(params(), config()) :: stream() | {:ok, raw_response(), String.t()} | {:error, String.t()}` and `@callback reask_messages(raw_response(), params(), config()) :: [map()]`. The reask callback is what makes the retry loop model-agnostic: each adapter reconstructs the prior assistant turn in its own wire format (e.g. an OpenAI `tool_calls` echo, an Anthropic `tool_use` block) so the follow-up error message threads correctly. `reask_messages/3` is only called if `function_exported?(adapter, :reask_messages, 3)`. Adapters present in lib/instructor/adapters: openai.ex, anthropic.ex, gemini.ex, ollama.ex, llamacpp.ex, groq.ex, vllm.ex, xai.ex. Most OpenAI-compatible providers (Groq, vLLM, Ollama, xAI) are thin OpenAI variants; Anthropic and Gemini have their own request/response shaping. The default mode is `:tools` precisely because both OpenAI and Anthropic expose structured output most reliably through tool/function calling — the JSON Schema becomes the tool's input schema.

JSON SCHEMA DERIVATION (`Instructor.JSONSchema.from_ecto_schema/1`). Documented caveat: "This will output a correct JSON Schema for the given Ecto schema, but it will not necessarily be optimal, nor support all Ecto types." It does a breadth-first traversal over the root schema and every embed/association, building a `%{title => schema}` map that becomes `$defs`; the root is either inlined or `$ref`'d depending on recursive references. `for_type/1` maps Ecto primitives to JSON Schema with inline example descriptions, e.g. `:integer -> %{type: "integer", description: "Integer, e.g. 1"}`, `:string -> %{type:"string", ...}`, `:boolean`, `:float -> %{type:"number", format:"float"}`, `:decimal -> %{type:"number", format:"float"}`, plus ISO8601 for temporal types. `Ecto.Enum` is matched as `{:parameterized, {Ecto.Enum, %{mappings: mappings}}} -> %{type:"string", enum: Keyword.keys(mappings)}`. Embeds/has_many become arrays of `$ref` to `#/$defs/Title`; has_one/embeds_one become a single `$ref`. Notably, ALL properties are emitted as `required` (`required = Map.keys(properties) |> Enum.sort()`) — there is no optional-field distinction in the schema, optionality is enforced (or not) only via changeset validation. The module-level `@llm_doc` string (falling back to legacy `@doc` via `fetch_ecto_schema_doc/1`) is embedded as the schema's top-level `description`, which is how per-field semantic hints reach the model (conventionally written as a markdown "## Field Descriptions" list inside `@llm_doc`).

VALIDATION SURFACE. `use Instructor.Validator` simply does `@behaviour Instructor.Validator` + `import Instructor.Validator`. The behaviour declares two optional callbacks: `validate_changeset(Ecto.Changeset.t) :: Ecto.Changeset.t` and `validate_changeset(Ecto.Changeset.t, map()) :: Ecto.Changeset.t`. Inside you use the full standard `Ecto.Changeset` validation vocabulary (`validate_number`, `validate_format`, `validate_inclusion`, `validate_required`, custom `add_error`, etc.). There is also `validate_with_llm/4` — a meta-validation helper that itself calls an LLM to judge a field against a natural-language rule (e.g. "must not say anything objectionable"), returning errors that then feed the same reask loop. Any error added in `validate_changeset` (code-based OR llm-based) participates identically in the `max_retries` reask cycle.

key_concepts.name: Ecto schema as the contract
key_concepts.what: An `embedded_schema` (usually `@primary_key false`) is the single source of truth: it defines the shape, drives JSON Schema generation for the request, and drives changeset casting/validation of the response. One declaration serves both the outbound prompt-schema and the inbound parse-check.

key_concepts.name: @llm_doc
key_concepts.what: A module attribute holding a markdown description (typically a '## Field Descriptions' list) that becomes the JSON Schema's `description`, conveying per-field semantics to the model. Falls back to `@doc`. This is the only place free-form field guidance lives.

key_concepts.name: validate_changeset/1,2 callback
key_concepts.what: Optional behaviour callback where you apply arbitrary `Ecto.Changeset` validations (and optionally `validate_with_llm`). Errors here are what trigger reasks. The /2 arity receives `validation_context` for runtime-dependent checks.

key_concepts.name: max_retries reask loop
key_concepts.what: On changeset invalidity, formatted errors + an adapter-specific echo of the prior assistant turn + a 'fix these errors' system message are appended and `chat_completion` recurses with `max_retries - 1`. This is the auto-coercion-via-conversation mechanism.

key_concepts.name: Instructor.Adapter behaviour
key_concepts.what: Two callbacks (`chat_completion/2`, `reask_messages/3`) abstract every backend. `reask_messages` keeps the retry loop wire-format-correct per provider. Adapters: OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Ollama, llamacpp, Groq, vLLM, xAI.

key_concepts.name: mode (:tools | :json | :md_json)
key_concepts.what: How the schema is delivered: as a tool/function input schema (default, best for OpenAI+Anthropic), as a native json/response_format, or embedded in markdown prompt for models lacking structured output. Determines where the derived JSON Schema is placed in the request.

key_concepts.name: from_ecto_schema/1
key_concepts.what: Generates JSON Schema via BFS over embeds/associations into `$defs`+`$ref`; maps Ecto primitives and `Ecto.Enum` (-> string enum); emits ALL fields as `required` (optionality is a changeset concern, not a schema concern); attaches `@llm_doc` as `description`.

api_or_code_examples.what: Canonical schema + validation + call (geex's exact target shape for a Command)
api_or_code_examples.snippet:
defmodule SpamPrediction do
  use Ecto.Schema
  use Instructor.Validator

  @llm_doc """
  ## Field Descriptions:
  - class: Whether or not the email is spam.
  - score: A confidence score between 0.0 and 1.0.
  """
  @primary_key false
  embedded_schema do
    field(:class, Ecto.Enum, values: [:spam, :not_spam])
    field(:score, :float)
  end

  @impl true
  def validate_changeset(changeset) do
    Ecto.Changeset.validate_number(changeset, :score,
      greater_than_or_equal_to: 0.0, less_than_or_equal_to: 1.0)
  end
end

Instructor.chat_completion(
  model: "gpt-4o-mini",
  response_model: SpamPrediction,
  max_retries: 3,
  messages: [%{role: "user", content: "..."}]
)
# => {:ok, %SpamPrediction{...}} | {:error, %Ecto.Changeset{}}

geex_relevance.what_to_take:
Two SEPARATE answers for the two directions.

DIRECTION A — geex CALLS an LLM (in-editor AI command, e.g. 'turn this prose into a geex macro', 'suggest a command'): VERDICT = ADAPT (lean toward ADOPT if geex is/becomes an Elixir app). This is exactly instructor_ex's wheelhouse: you want a validated Elixir struct out of a model. If geex's runtime is Elixir, depend on instructor_ex directly — define an Ecto embedded_schema for the AI command's expected output, get `{:ok, struct}` with free retries. If geex is NOT Elixir, adapt the *technique*, not the library: (schema -> JSON Schema -> cast -> validate -> on-error reask with formatted errors). The single most valuable, language-portable idea is the reask loop: format validation errors as text, append them + the model's prior tool-call echo, decrement a retry budget, recurse. Steal that wholesale.

DIRECTION B — an LLM CALLS geex (MCP tool export of geex commands; inbound tool-call args must become a Command struct): VERDICT = REFERENCE the technique, do NOT adopt the library. The boundary instructor_ex defines — 'JSON Schema out, validated struct (with coercion + retries) in' — IS geex's MCP validation boundary, so the *pattern* maps perfectly. But the source-of-truth conflicts: instructor_ex makes an Ecto schema the authority and DERIVES JSON Schema from it; geex already has a macro-DSL command definition as its authority and would DERIVE both the MCP inputSchema AND the arg-validator from THAT. You don't want a parallel Ecto schema per command duplicating the DSL. So reference three concrete techniques and reimplement against the geex command AST: (1) the type->JSON-Schema mapping table and the $defs/$ref BFS for nested args; (2) a cast/coerce step that turns loosely-typed inbound JSON (string '3' -> integer 3, string -> enum atom) into typed Command fields — Ecto.Changeset.cast is the model, but geex can do it directly off DSL arg specs; (3) the error-feedback reask loop *if* geex controls the calling agent — though for pure MCP-server export, geex usually does NOT control the retry (the calling LLM/host owns retries), so the reask loop is mostly N/A for Direction B; instead return MCP `isError: true` with the formatted validation errors and let the host model self-correct. One caveat to copy deliberately AVOIDING: instructor_ex marks every field `required` in the JSON Schema and pushes optionality into validation — for MCP export geex should emit proper `required` arrays so the calling model gets accurate hints.
geex_relevance.how_it_composes: Fits geex's 'commands-as-data + macro DSL + one dispatcher for human and LLM' model cleanly IF geex keeps the macro DSL as the single source of truth and treats instructor_ex as a pattern, not a schema owner. Because geex already has one dispatcher serving humans and LLMs, the validated Command struct from the MCP path should be byte-identical to the one a human keystroke path produces — instructor_ex's '{:ok, struct} | {:error, changeset}' contract is a good shape to mirror so both callers converge on the same Command. The CONFLICT to manage: do not let an Ecto schema become a second, competing definition of a command alongside the DSL; that would split the source of truth and break the 'commands-as-data' invariant. The reask loop composes naturally only in Direction A (geex driving the model); in Direction B the host owns retries, so geex's job is just accurate schema-out + good error-strings-in-MCP-errors.
